title: Architecture
description: Architecture of the Deccan — Bahmani fortresses, Qutb Shahi minarets, Adil Shahi domes.
dedication: In memory of the Asaf Jahi dynasty
subtitle: Bahmani fortresses, Qutb Shahi minarets, Adil Shahi domes

sections.sub: A third Indo-Islamic tradition that still imported its masters from Iran
body: The Deccan school is a third great Indo-Islamic tradition, distinct from the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal style. Its early monuments are Bahmani — the great Jami mosque at Gulbarga (1367), the painted tile-work of Bidar, the soaring Mahmud Gawan madrasa with its chequered turquoise faïence. They speak of an outward-looking court that still imported masters from Iran.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

aside.label: Five monuments to know

items.value: Hyderabad, 1591 — Quli Qutb Shah's four-minaret arch at the heart of the new city.
Granite citadel with the famed acoustic gateway: a clap at the entrance reaches the durbar.
Bijapur, 1656 — second-largest unsupported dome in the world; whisper carries seven echoes.
Triple-moated Bahmani citadel; sixteen gates, four palaces, the Rangin Mahal in painted tile.
South Asia's most complete royal necropolis — every Golconda sultan in one walled garden.

aside.note: Indo-Persian arches, Vijayanagara columns, Persian tilework and Telugu masons — Deccan architecture is the clearest evidence of a hybrid civilisation.

sections.sub: A smaller, more elegant style — the Charminar and the royal necropolis
body: The Qutb Shahis at Golconda and Hyderabad invented their own idiom: smaller, more elegant, fond of stucco arabesques and onion domes. The Charminar (1591) was both a triumphal arch over the new city and a working mosque on its upper floor. North of the city, twenty-one royal tombs stand in a single garden — every Golconda sultan and many of their queens — the largest Qutb Shahi necropolis in the world.<cite data-ref="britannica-charminar britannica-golconda"></cite>

sections.sub: Where the Adil Shahis went furthest — the Taj of the Deccan
body: At Bijapur the Adil Shahis went furthest. The Gol Gumbaz, built for Muhammad Adil Shah in the 1650s, holds an unsupported dome 44 metres across; a whisper at one corner of its gallery is heard with perfect clarity at the opposite corner, seven times over. Across town the Ibrahim Rauza, the lyrical tomb of Ibrahim II, has been called the Taj of the Deccan — and it predates the Taj Mahal by twenty years.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

items.text: With the founding of the Bahmani Sultanate, the first dedicated Deccani architectural idiom emerges — drawing on Persian forms, local granite, and craftsmen imported from Iran.

The great Jami mosque at Gulbarga is completed: one of the earliest surviving monuments of the Deccan school, its arcaded courtyard covering the prayer hall entirely.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>
The Bidar fort complex develops under the Bahmanis — triple moats, sixteen gates, four palaces, and the Rangin Mahal with its painted tile interior.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

The Mahmud Gawan madrasa at Bidar is built with its chequered turquoise faïence facade — the most ambitious example of Bahmani Persian tilework and the Deccan's leading centre of learning.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah builds the Charminar at the centre of the new city of Hyderabad — a four-minaret arch serving as both a triumphal gateway and a working mosque on its upper floor.<cite data-ref="britannica-charminar"></cite>

The Qutb Shahi necropolis north of Golconda grows to twenty-one royal tombs in a single walled garden — South Asia's most complete royal necropolis, housing every Golconda sultan and many of their queens.<cite data-ref="britannica-golconda"></cite>

The Ibrahim Rauza at Bijapur — the tomb and mosque of Ibrahim Adil Shah II — is completed; its lyrical proportions earn it the epithet 'Taj of the Deccan,' predating the completion of the Taj Mahal by more than two decades.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

Muhammad Adil Shah's Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur is completed: an unsupported dome 44 metres across, ringed by a whispering gallery where a whisper carries seven clear echoes.<cite data-ref="britannica-gol-gumbaz"></cite>
The Deccani synthesis of Indo-Persian arches, Persian tilework, Vijayanagara columns, and Telugu masonry is the clearest built evidence of the region's hybrid civilisation.

references.text: George Michell & Mark Zebrowski, Architecture and Art of the Deccan Sultanates (The New Cambridge History of India I.7), Cambridge University Press, 1999.
